title: Success is Planned

tactic.name: Template Your Engineering
tactic.one_liner: Encode your engineering workflows and best practices into reusable templates — meta-prompts that generate plans — so agents can ship whole classes of work (chores, bugs, features) with your team's standards, over and over, on any size codebase.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: Three separate discomforts. First, planning was the engineer's sacred craft — the thing you did BECAUSE you'd stopped typing code — and this tactic hands even the plan-writing to the agent ('let our agents write the first and sometimes final draft of our plans'). Second, it demands you throw away the conversation: fresh, memory-less agent instances for every phase instead of one long omniscient session — Dan pre-acknowledges it on camera: 'I know this looks weird. I know it might feel uncomfortable. We don't see our agent.' Third, templates are an upfront investment that produces zero code on day one; you're paying engineering time to encode process, trusting the payoff arrives across hundreds of agent executions.

mission: Scale your prompts into plans and your plans into templates — entering the plan-and-build phase of the agentic software development lifecycle. With just three tactics (Stop Coding, Adopt Your Agent's Perspective, Template Your Engineering) you get the Pareto 80/20 of agentic engineering, and you unlock the ability to not just augment but automate the entire SDLC with agents shipping work on your behalf. 'Those who plan the future tend to create it. Success is planned.'

scaling_ladder.prompt: The unit of communication with all generative AI — 'what was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have.' A high-level prompt is deliberately 'void of detail': one sentence that names the outcome.
scaling_ladder.plan: A prompt scaled up for high impact: 'It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD.' The plan IS the prompt — great planning is great prompting. Plans are 'staging environments for code': engineering work compressed into natural language that the agent expands into code.
scaling_ladder.template: A reusable meta-prompt that generates plans in a fixed markdown format. Templates encode HOW your team solves each class of problem (chore/bug/feature) so 'you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve' the encoded practice. One of the 12 leverage points of agentic coding.
scaling_ladder.higher_order_prompt: A prompt that accepts other prompts as input parameters (/implement takes a plan file path). On-screen definition: 'A prompt that accepts other prompts as input parameters, enabling composable agentic workflows... like passing functions into functions in programming languages, but for agentic systems.'
scaling_ladder.programmatic_invocation: The same slash-command templates fired headlessly via claude -p with streamed JSONL output — the lesson-ending bridge to AI developer workflows (ADWs) and true off-device agentic coding in lesson 4.

core_concepts.name: The prompt is everything
core_concepts.plain_english: The prompt is the medium through which you communicate with agentic tools and all generative AI. Prompting skill compounds into everything else in TAC: adopting your agent's perspective is empathy work — understanding exactly what the agent sees so your communication lands.
core_concepts.dan_words: "What was once a complete joke is now the most valuable skill any engineer can have. The prompt is everything."
core_concepts.misconception: That prompt engineering was a fad that died. It didn't die — it graduated. Prompts scaled up became plans, specs, and PRDs; the skill got renamed 'planning' and became the core of the agentic SDLC.

core_concepts.name: Plans are prompts scaled up
core_concepts.plain_english: Ask 'what does a scaled prompt look like?' and the answer is a plan / specification / PRD. A plan is not documentation about the work — it IS the executable instruction for the work, written in natural language the agent expands into code. Full circle: great planning is great prompting.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD. Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact. The plan is the prompt... great planning is great prompting."
core_concepts.misconception: That plans are inert docs for humans that go stale in a wiki. In TAC the plan is fired INTO an agent as the prompt (via /implement); saving plans to specs/ turns them into referenceable, improvable codebase artifacts for you, your team, and your agents.

core_concepts.name: Tactic #3: Template Your Engineering
core_concepts.plain_english: Encode your problem-solving patterns into reusable template files that generate plans. You solve the CLASS of problem once (how we do chores; how we fix bugs; how we build features) instead of re-deriving the approach per instance. Templates work small-to-large: chores, bugs, small and large features, new codebases, up to massive refactors — and they're one of the named solutions to 'my codebase is too big.'
core_concepts.dan_words: "When you template your engineering, you encode your problem solving into reusable units that you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve."
core_concepts.misconception: That 'template' means code boilerplate or snippets. These templates contain no application code at all — they encode PROCESS: instructions, focus files, a plan format, and a parameter slot. The output of a template isn't code; it's a plan.

core_concepts.name: The meta prompt — a prompt that builds a prompt
core_concepts.plain_english: /chore, /bug, and /feature are meta prompts: agentic prompts that build a plan based on a template the agent fills out. You type one high-level sentence; the agent researches the codebase (starting with README.md), THINKs HARD, and writes a complete plan into specs/. The demo turned a one-sentence chore into a 64-line plan.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is a template and a meta prompt. What is a meta prompt? It's a prompt that builds a prompt. More specifically, this agentic prompt builds a plan based on a template that our agent fills out."
core_concepts.misconception: That firing /chore solves the chore. It doesn't touch the application code — it only PLANS. The plan-then-build split into two separate agent runs is the whole point (planning phase and coding phase are different SDLC nodes with different context needs).

core_concepts.name: The Higher Order Prompt (HOP)
core_concepts.plain_english: /implement is a prompt that takes another prompt (the plan file) as its argument — 'plans getting passed into plans.' Like higher-order functions in programming, HOPs make prompts composable: the same 12-line implement.md runs ANY spec you generate, and you can write HOP variants (implement-then-review-against-plan, etc.) that shape work without touching the templates.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is a higher order prompt, AKA a hop." On-screen definition: "A prompt that accepts other prompts as input parameters, enabling composable agentic workflows. Higher order prompts (HOPs) allow you to pass plans, templates, or other prompts into reusable execution frameworks - like passing functions into functions in programming languages, but for agentic systems."
core_concepts.misconception: That implement.md must be big to be powerful. It is 12 lines: purpose, one instruction ('Read the plan, think hard about the plan and implement the plan.'), a ## Plan section holding $ARGUMENTS, and a ## Report block. The power is in what flows THROUGH it, not what's in it — 'It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information.'

core_concepts.name: Anatomy of a template (and where plans live)
core_concepts.plain_english: Every template in the lesson has the same skeleton: a purpose line at the top; ## Instructions (be thorough, name the file appropriately, replace every <placeholder>, THINK HARD, start research at README.md); ## Relevant Files (focus on README, app/**, scripts/** — ignore everything else); ## Plan Format (the exact markdown skeleton the plan must follow, in a ```md block); and a final section holding $ARGUMENTS where your one-line request lands. All generated plans are written to the specs/ directory.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Create a new plan in the specs directory to resolve the chore using the specified plan format... We are giving our agent a template... our last section is just chore with the Claude Code argument parameter that just takes whatever we passed in."
core_concepts.misconception: That one plan format fits all work. The three templates deliberately differ: bug.md adds Problem/Solution Statements, Steps to Reproduce, and Root Cause Analysis; feature.md adds User Story, a 3-phase Implementation Plan, Testing Strategy, and Acceptance Criteria; chore.md stays minimal. Different classes of engineering work get different encoded processes.

core_concepts.name: THINK HARD — turning on the reasoning model
core_concepts.plain_english: The templates and implement.md embed the phrase 'think hard' — an information-dense keyword Anthropic encoded into Claude Code that activates the reasoning model. Dan frames it as one of the 12 leverage points: you always want to throw more compute at the problem as the work scales.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Read the plan. Think hard. We're activating Claude Code's information dense keyword to activate the reasoning model... We always wanna throw more compute at the problem."
core_concepts.misconception: That 'think hard' is superstition. In course-era Claude Code it is a documented trigger tier for extended thinking (think < think hard < ultrathink); the specific magic words are tool-version-dependent, but the underlying lever — explicitly buying more reasoning compute for planning — is real and current.

core_concepts.name: Fresh agents, one task each — three reasons
core_concepts.plain_english: Dan keeps opening brand-new Claude Code instances (new terminal, zero memory) for every phase: plan, implement, next plan. Reason 1: focus — every available token goes to the task at hand (agents have context windows like overloaded humans; the more focused, the better the result). Reason 2: it forces your prompts, plans, and templates to be isolated, reusable, improvable assets with zero dependencies on conversation history. Reason 3: it prepares you for true off-device agentic coding, where no conversation exists at all.
core_concepts.dan_words: "By running fresh agents over and over... we free up our context... we force our prompts, plans and templates to be isolated, reusable, and improvable assets with zero dependencies... and most importantly... we prepare for true off-device agentic coding."
core_concepts.misconception: That rolling one long conversation across planning and building is safer because the agent 'remembers.' The memory is the liability: it hides dependencies your assets silently rely on, degrades focus on large codebases, and cannot exist in headless/off-device runs. 'We need to decouple our performance from the conversational context window.'

core_concepts.name: Knowing your agent's perspective at boot
core_concepts.plain_english: When a fresh agent starts from /implement plus a plan file, you know 100% of its context: it read implement.md, it read the plan, it went to work. That certainty gives you a trail of success — when something goes wrong you know exactly which asset (template, plan, or HOP) to improve, and as your codebase grows you specialize templates for specific systems and classes of bugs. This is also lesson 2's KPIs operationalized: size of handed-off work up, attempts down, streak up, presence toward zero — via one-shot successes.
core_concepts.dan_words: "When I set this up, I know 100%... what the agent's perspective is... We want one shot successes... Remember, we're not here to babysit a single agent."
core_concepts.misconception: That one-shotting means small work. 'That doesn't mean that our agents do a ton of work — that's the whole point — size goes up. But it does mean that our plans — our prompts scaled up — contain everything an agent needs to get started.'

core_concepts.name: Validation commands — plans that check themselves
core_concepts.plain_english: Every plan format ends with a Validation Commands section ('Execute every command to validate... with zero regressions' — e.g. cd app/server && uv run pytest) and the step-by-step tasks end by running them. On camera the implement agent runs the tests, runs a git diff over its own work, finds two issues, and fixes them without being asked. Bug plans additionally include Steps to Reproduce so humans can verify too.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We have several self-validating loops with tests... It's checking its own work — self validation. It has two issues it needs to fix here. It's going to fix them automatically... I still haven't lifted a finger."
core_concepts.misconception: That you can skip the manual check because the agent self-validates. Dan still restarts the server, re-runs queries in the browser, greps for leftover print statements, and runs pytest himself — self-validation shrinks review, it doesn't delete it. (Closing the loop gets its own dedicated lesson later.)

core_concepts.name: claude -p + stream-json — the off-device preview
core_concepts.plain_english: The finale wraps /feature in Claude Code's programmatic form and runs it with no visible agent: claude -p "/feature \"...\"" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus --verbose > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl. The JSONL file appends live — system init, assistant messages, tool results — while the agent plans a whole feature in the background. 'You can imagine this command is running on any machine anywhere.' This is the planning phase of the SDLC running without you: the seed of AI developer workflows (lesson 4).
core_concepts.dan_words: "We want this to run on its own in a box on some device somewhere else... This prompt here represents the planning phase... so that our agents are operating this for us."
core_concepts.misconception: That the JSONL is just a log file. It's the agent's entire output stream as machine-readable events — the interface another program (or another agent) consumes to chain agents together: 'we can chain these agents together. We can check their output.'

core_concepts.name: Templates as team leverage and differentiation
core_concepts.plain_english: Templates are time savers 'not just for you, but for your entire team' — encoded once, executed infinitely, and improvable by everyone (the /install command itself reuses a scripted prompt to copy .env from tac-2 — reuse all the way down). Off-the-shelf tools (Codex, Copilot, Devin, Jules, Gemini CLI 'and whatever comes next') don't understand your codebase like you do and don't give you this granularity of control; custom templates are how your engineering — and product — differentiates.
core_concepts.dan_words: "These tools are great, but they're limited by nature. No matter how great AI gets, they don't understand your codebase like you do... The more custom your templates are, the more unique your engineering gets."
core_concepts.misconception: That generic chore/bug/feature templates are the end state. They're 'high level generic units, generic classes of engineering work' — the real power arrives when you specialize: a front-end feature template for specific pages, a chore template for your database migration system, a bug resolver for your research-notebook system.

core_concepts.name: 'My codebase is too big' is a limiting belief
core_concepts.plain_english: The lesson pre-handles the biggest objection: templating works on small to large codebases and is explicitly 'one of many solutions to the my-codebase-is-too-big problem' — the bigger and more complex the codebase, the MORE you want dialed-in reusable templates (plus tricks layered on later: parallel agents, delegation, isolated subagent context windows). Betting against this is betting against improving models and tools.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Don't make the mistake of thinking that this is not going to work for your system, for your codebase... that is a limiting belief. Models will improve. Tools will change. These tactics are ultra, ultra useful."
core_concepts.misconception: That you should finish the course before trying it. Dan's call to action is the opposite: 'Do not wait... Run /chore and just do something small. Don't wait to complete this course. You'll miss out on getting ahead now.'

templates_suite.common_skeleton: All three planning templates share: purpose line ('Create a new plan in specs/*.md to resolve/implement the X using the exact specified markdown Plan Format') → ## Instructions (thoroughness, naming, replace every <placeholder>, 'Use your reasoning model: THINK HARD', respect Relevant Files, start research at README.md) → ## Relevant Files (README.md, app/**, scripts/** — 'Ignore all other files in the codebase.') → ## Plan Format (exact markdown skeleton in a ```md fence) → final H2 holding $ARGUMENTS.
templates_suite.chore_md: 53 lines. Plan format: Chore name / Chore Description / Relevant Files (+ optional H3 'New Files') / Step by Step Tasks ('IMPORTANT: Execute every step in order, top to bottom.') / Validation Commands (seeded with `cd app/server && uv run pytest`, 'Don't validate with curl commands.') / Notes. Tone: 'it should be simple but we need to be thorough and precise so we don't miss anything or waste time with any second round of changes.'
templates_suite.bug_md: 69 lines. Adds to the chore skeleton: Bug Description (symptoms, expected vs actual), Problem Statement, Solution Statement, Steps to Reproduce, Root Cause Analysis. Extra instructions: 'Be surgical with your bug fix', 'minimal number of changes', 'Don't use decorators. Keep it simple.', use `uv add` for new libraries and report them in Notes, include repro commands before and after the fix in validation.
templates_suite.feature_md: 91 lines. Adds: Feature Description, User Story (As a / I want to / So that), Problem + Solution Statements, 3-phase Implementation Plan (Foundation / Core Implementation / Integration), Testing Strategy (Unit / Integration / Edge Cases), Acceptance Criteria. Extra instructions: research existing patterns first, 'Follow existing patterns and conventions... Don't reinvent the wheel', design for extensibility. Relevant Files splits app/server/** and app/client/**.
templates_suite.implement_md: 12 lines (the file's last line has no trailing newline, so `wc -l` reports 11 — Dan's on-camera count of 12 matches what the editor displays). Purpose → single instruction ('Read the plan, think hard about the plan and implement the plan.') → ## Plan holding $ARGUMENTS → ## Report ('Summarize the work you've just done in a concise bullet point list' + 'Report the files and total lines changed with `git diff --stat`'). The universal executor: one HOP runs every spec the templates generate.

fresh_agents_doctrine.reason_1_focus: Free up your context — focus every available token on the task at hand. Important for large codebases and long-running tasks; one agent, one task, one mission. 'We as humans, we also have context windows... the more we focus, the better the result.'
fresh_agents_doctrine.reason_2_zero_dependencies: Force your prompts, plans, and templates to be isolated, reusable, improvable assets with zero dependencies. Because you EXPECT to run fresh instances, nothing can silently depend on conversation history — which is what makes templates shareable and improvable ('a trail of success or a trail of things we can improve').
fresh_agents_doctrine.reason_3_off_device: Prepare for true off-device agentic coding. 'We're not here to babysit a single agent' — improve the KPIs (size ↑, attempts ↓, streak ↑, presence → 0) by kicking off new instances at the right node of the SDLC with no previous context: 'we need to decouple our performance from the conversational context window'; aim for one-shot successes where the plan contains everything the agent needs.
fresh_agents_doctrine.observed_in_demo: Separate instances for: /install setup, /chore planning, /implement (chore), /bug planning, /implement (bug), and the headless claude -p /feature run — six agent boots in one lesson, with Dan committing specs + code between phases so 'each one of these steps commits their changes' (full Git discipline promised in upcoming lessons).

programmatic_preview.why_it_matters: To build features end-to-end without opening a terminal, the agent must run without you being there — and because Claude Code runs in the terminal, it can run anywhere a terminal exists (local, cloud, 'in a box on some device somewhere else'). The lesson ends by firing the /feature template through claude -p in exactly the shape lesson 4's AI developer workflows will scale: template + headless invocation + streamed machine-readable output.
programmatic_preview.command_verbatim:
claude -p "/feature \"Create a new query history side panel in the app. This shows all completed queries. Store in the database. order by newest first. Use a new llm call to generate names for each query we'll display in the side panel. When we click we refocus the main panel on the query. Add a 'show panel' button next to 'upload data'\"" \
  --output-format stream-json \
  --dangerously-skip-permissions \
  --model opus \
  --verbose \
  > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl

flags_explained.-p: Programmatic (print) mode — run the prompt headlessly and exit.
flags_explained.--output-format stream-json: Emit the agent's activity as streaming JSON events (one JSON object per line → JSONL file): system init, assistant messages, tool results.
flags_explained.--dangerously-skip-permissions: Skip permission prompts entirely. Dan: 'This is going to work just fine for now. It's very low risk' — acceptable for a planning-only run in a demo repo; the flag name is the warning.
flags_explained.--model opus: Pin the model. The stream shows claude-opus-4-20250514 — 'running on whatever the best model is. So you're operating in the future, whatever your best model is, use that.'
flags_explained.--verbose: Include the full event stream (needed for stream-json detail).
flags_explained.> feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl: Redirect the stream to a file you can tail live, parse, or hand to another agent — 'we can chain these agents together. We can check their output.'

programmatic_preview.observed_output: feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl appends live during the run (line 22... 23... 24 on camera). Events visible: {"type":"system","subtype":"init",...}, assistant messages with model claude-opus-4-20250514, user tool_result entries ('Todos have been modified'). Result: specs/query-history-panel.md written by a background agent — reviewed on screen, deliberately NOT implemented ('I'm not gonna run this right now').

loot_box_mentions: Lesson 3 ships 22 loot notes; the two on-screen loot box pointers are the lesson-3 repository clone link and the closing 'review some of the resources available to you in your loot box below.'
Command notes: /chore "your chore description" and /implement specs/your-plan.md

Idea notes distilling the lesson: The Prompt is Everything; Plans Are Scaled Prompts; Success is Planned; The 80-20 of Agentic Coding; Tactic #3 Template Your Engineering; Solving Problem Classes Not Problems; Templates for Team Leverage; Planning Alone is Expensive; Templates Encode Problem Solving; Reusable Prompts as Time Savers; Meta-Prompts (prompts that build prompts); Plans Written to Specs Directory; Built-in Validation Commands; From One Line to Comprehensive Plan; Anatomy of a Template; Now We Can Template Our Engineering; Activating Reasoning with 'Think Hard'; Higher-Order Prompts (HOPs); Aligning Plans with Agent Capabilities.
step_by_step_demo: (5:20–5:47) Clone the lesson-3 repo (loot box link), cd in, open VS Code; boot Claude Code and fire /install — note install.md now runs ./scripts/copy_dot_env.sh to copy the .env from your tac-2 directory ('a quick way to reuse resources... having an agent with a reusable prompt do this work for us').
(6:02–6:20) Open install.md and scripts/copy_dot_env.sh to see exactly what the setup command does; agent reports .env copied, backend + frontend dependencies installed.

(6:46–7:45) New terminal: scripts/start.sh → backend :8000 + frontend :5173. In the browser: Upload Data → users.json; query 'Show users with age between 20 and 40' — works as in lesson 2; stdout logging visible in the terminal (foreshadowing the chore).

(7:47–8:06) Fresh Claude Code instance: /chore "Replace all server print statements with proper python logging. Use proper log levels. Preserve the exact same log output. Make sure all output is written standard out" (as typed on screen). 'This is a template and a meta prompt... a prompt that builds a plan based on a template that our agent fills out.'

(8:10–9:42) Watch the agent research the codebase with its reasoning model, then Write specs/replace-print-with-logging.md — 64 lines from one sentence. The plan inventories every print by line number (18 lines in server.py + 1 in main.py; the agent's own summary text says '19 print statements' in server.py / '20 across 2 files' — its prose miscounts its own correct inventory by one).

(9:42–9:58) Open the generated plan in preview: Chore / Chore Description / Relevant Files / Step by Step Tasks / Validation Commands / Notes — 'this lines up with exactly what was generated' from the template's Plan Format.

(9:58–11:58) Open .claude/commands/chore.md and dissect the template: purpose at top, Instructions (THINK HARD), Relevant Files, Plan Format in a ```md fence, and the ## Chore section holding $ARGUMENTS — 'takes our string and places it down here.'
(12:30–12:44) NEW fresh instance: /implement + paste the plan path. 'It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information.'

(13:07–13:40) Crack open implement.md while it runs: 12 lines — read the plan, think hard (reasoning model on, a 12-leverage-points lever), yolo/auto-accept mode for edits; ## Plan $ARGUMENTS makes it 'a higher order prompt, AKA a hop... plans getting passed into plans.'

(14:00–15:45) The agent's todo list lines up 1:1 with the plan's Step by Step Tasks ('we're aligning it with the capabilities of our agent'); the Report block executes: bullet summary + git diff --stat of files changed.

(15:25–17:20) Validation: the plan's commands run (cd app/server && uv run pytest + running server and main); review git diff yourself (print(f"[SUCCESS]...") → logger.info(f"[SUCCESS]..."), errors → logger.error with exc_info/format_exc); restart the app, run 'get users id name sorted by signup date descending', confirm the new logging format; regex-search the codebase for print( — all logging/logger now.
(17:44–19:09) Fresh instance again: /bug "resolve major issue, our SQL statements not being escaped, user input into SQL" (as narrated). Same pattern: meta prompt + template → plan.

(19:25–21:30) While it thinks (thinking mode = throw more compute at the problem), recap the leverage points at work: templates, agent perspective, reasoning mode, core four, a well-designed simple client/server codebase, README documentation.

(21:00–22:20) Review specs/fix-sql-injection-vulnerabilities.md: Bug Description, Problem/Solution Statements, Steps to Reproduce (start app, send malicious input), Root Cause Analysis (keyword blocklist assumed sufficient; table/column names trusted from uploaded files; SQLite parameter binding doesn't cover identifiers → f-string interpolation; no centralized SQL execution layer), Relevant Files (sql_processor.py executes without parameterization; file_processor.py + insights.py f-string table/column names; server.py has a DROP TABLE f-string in the delete_table endpoint — all four verified real in the course codebase), plus H3 New Files: app/server/core/sql_security.py.

(22:20–22:50) Commit the pending specs + code ('you want each one of these steps to commit their changes' — full Git discipline in upcoming lessons), then in a NEW instance: /implement + the bug plan path.

(23:02–28:10) THE explanation: why fresh agents every time — (1) free up context/focus every token, (2) prompts/plans/templates become isolated, reusable, improvable, zero-dependency assets, (3) prepare for true off-device agentic coding; KPIs: increase size of work handed off, decrease attempts, increase streak, drive presence to zero; 'decouple our performance from the conversational context window'; one-shot successes; the ~100-line plan contains everything the agent needs; you know 100% of the agent's perspective at boot (implement.md + plan file).

(29:40–30:30) HOPs generalize: write implement variants ('after you implement, review the work completed against the plan') — higher order activity over any spec. The bug agent runs its own git diff, finds 2 issues in its work, fixes them automatically: 'I still haven't lifted a finger.'

(32:55–33:47) Open a blank file and draft the /feature prompt (query history side panel). Meanwhile the bug implement finishes: 52 tests pass on camera including 18 new SQL-injection prevention tests, a new test file, README security-section updates.

(34:00–35:20) Manually verify the bug fix: try a concat/injection-shaped query in the UI, exercise upload/hide, then cd app/server && uv run pytest yourself. 'This is why it's important to have steps to reproduce inside of the plan.'

(36:27–37:44) Wrap the /feature prompt in programmatic form — claude -p "/feature \"...\"" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus --verbose > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl — fire it in the terminal, and watch the JSONL append live (line 22 → 23 → 24): an invisible agent doing the planning phase of the SDLC.

(38:05–39:00) Open .claude/commands/feature.md — 'You can always read the purpose right at the top of the prompt' — same meta-prompt pattern specialized for net-new features. 'This is where a lot of your key essential engineering time and resources will be spent. You want to be building the system that builds the system.'

(41:00–43:20) The background agent finishes: specs/query-history-panel.md — Feature Description, User Story (as a data analyst...), Problem/Solution, Relevant Files, 3-phase Implementation Plan, Step by Step Tasks, Testing Strategy, Acceptance Criteria, Validation Commands. Reviewed, deliberately not implemented.

(43:49–44:30) Call to action: 'Do not wait... open up a chore, copy this right into your codebase... run /chore and just do something small' — get to the aha moment now; 'my codebase is too big' is a limiting belief.

(44:30–46:32) Recap over the 8-tactics stack: stop coding → adopt your agent's perspective → template your engineering; lesson 4 teaser: programmatic agents, triggers, agents running in their own environments — AI developer workflows, 'the highest composition level and the greatest leverage point of agentic coding'... 'let your product ship itself.'

It's a plan. It's a specification. It's a PRD. Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact.
The plan is the prompt. And that means great planning is great prompting.
Those who plan the future tend to create it. Success is planned.
With just three tactics, you'll learn the Pareto 80/20 of agentic engineering.
When you template your engineering, you encode your problem solving into reusable units that you, your team, and your agents can see, use, and importantly, improve.
What is a meta prompt? It's a prompt that builds a prompt.
Not only should we stop coding, we should also lean into and leverage our agent to write plans with us and for us.
It doesn't take a lot to do a lot, but you need the right information.
This is a higher order prompt, AKA a hop.
Don't limit yourself. Don't make the mistake in thinking that Gen AI can't solve your problem in a major way.

This is the power of templating your engineering. I still haven't lifted a finger.
Having agents run loose on your code base without structure, without knowing how you do things is a plan for failure.
You want to be building the system that builds the system.
You can also think of your plans as staging environments for code that will be generated.
Be very careful thinking that these tactics can't work for you and on your codebase. That is a limiting belief.
I'll see you in lesson four where we'll learn to let your product ship itself.

An OpenAI or Anthropic API key for the app's NL→SQL feature (app/server/.env)
The tac-2 repo cloned as a sibling directory IF you want /install's copy_dot_env.sh step to work (it copies ../tac-2/app/server/.env); otherwise cp app/server/.env.sample and fill keys manually
An IDE (Dan uses VS Code) and a browser for localhost:5173
what_student_must_internalize: The plan IS the prompt. A plan/spec/PRD is a prompt scaled up for high impact — so great planning is literally great prompting, not a separate discipline.
Templates encode problem-solving for CLASSES of work, not instances. /chore, /bug, /feature each encode a different process; the output of a template is always a plan in specs/, never code.
A meta prompt is a prompt that builds a prompt; a higher order prompt (HOP) is a prompt that takes prompts as input. Template → plan → /implement(plan) is meta-prompting composed with a HOP.

Two prompts, two phases, two agents: planning and building are separate SDLC nodes run by separate fresh instances. The chore was completed 'agentically with two prompts, one for the planning phase and one for the coding building phase.'

The three reasons for fresh agents: context focus; isolated/reusable/improvable zero-dependency assets; preparation for off-device runs. Decouple performance from the conversational context window; aim for one-shot successes.
At boot you should know 100% of your agent's context (the HOP file + the plan file). That certainty is what makes failures diagnosable and templates improvable.
Plans embed their own validation (Validation Commands + tests + steps-to-reproduce); agents can and do check their own work — but you still manually verify.
THINK HARD–style reasoning activation is a leverage point: deliberately buy more compute for planning-grade work.
The same slash-command template runs interactively AND headlessly (claude -p + stream-json → JSONL). That symmetry is the bridge from this lesson to AI developer workflows.
Start now, small: run /chore on something real today; 'my codebase is too big' is a named limiting belief, and specialization of templates is the answer to scale.
common_weak_student_failures: Running /chore and then telling the SAME session to 'go ahead and do it' — collapsing the plan/build split and never producing the reusable plan artifact (the plan is the deliverable of phase one; /implement in a fresh instance is phase two).

Treating the generated plan as read-only. The plan is a staging environment — Dan explicitly leaves room to 'iterate on' plans before firing /implement; weak students fire immediately and blame the template.

Keeping one long conversation 'so the agent has context,' then wondering why the same prompt behaves differently next week — they built a hidden dependency on conversation history instead of a zero-dependency asset.

Editing generated code by hand when the implement run misses something, instead of improving the template/plan and re-running — destroying the trail of success the system is designed to create ('you're probably going to miss something... tweak it' refers to the TEMPLATE).
Copying the templates verbatim into their own repo without changing the Relevant Files section — the agent then researches README.md/app/**/scripts/** that don't exist and produces vague plans.
Skipping the Validation Commands section (or leaving the pytest seed line pointing at a directory their repo doesn't have) — plans stop being self-checking and regressions slip through silently.
Reading 'dangerously-skip-permissions' as the default way to run headless everywhere, missing that Dan scoped it to a low-risk planning-only run in a demo repo.
Waiting to 'finish the course first' instead of running one small /chore today — missing the aha moment the lesson is engineered to produce.

Assuming the video's exact counts must match their run ('the video got 52 tests, I got 49, something's broken') — generated plans and tests vary run to run; the pass criterion is zero regressions plus new coverage, not a magic number.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) the scaling ladder from prompt → plan → template → higher order prompt, defining meta prompt and HOP in one sentence each, with /chore and /implement as your evidence; (2) the three reasons Dan boots a fresh, memory-less agent for every phase, and what 'decouple performance from the conversational context window' means for one-shot successes; (3) how a generated plan validates itself (name the two mechanisms: embedded Validation Commands and the agent's own diff-review), and what Dan still checks manually; and (4) what changes — and what stays identical — when the /feature template is fired via claude -p with stream-json instead of interactively. Finish by resolving the title: in what concrete, non-motivational sense is success 'planned' in this system?

retrieval_questions.q: What does a scaled prompt look like, in Dan's exact terms?
retrieval_questions.a: A plan. A specification. A PRD. 'Plans are prompts scaled up for high impact' — the plan is the prompt, so great planning is great prompting.

retrieval_questions.q: Define a meta prompt and name the three in the lesson codebase.
retrieval_questions.a: A prompt that builds a prompt — specifically an agentic prompt that builds a plan from a template the agent fills out. /chore (chore.md), /bug (bug.md), /feature (feature.md).

retrieval_questions.q: Define a higher order prompt (HOP) and give the lesson's example.
retrieval_questions.a: A prompt that accepts other prompts as input parameters — like passing functions into functions, but for agentic systems. /implement takes a plan file path in its ## Plan $ARGUMENTS slot: plans passed into prompts.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the five structural parts every template in the lesson shares.
retrieval_questions.a: Purpose line at top; ## Instructions (including THINK HARD and 'start research by reading README.md'); ## Relevant Files ('Ignore all other files'); ## Plan Format (exact markdown skeleton in a ```md fence); a final section holding $ARGUMENTS.

retrieval_questions.q: Where do all generated plans go, and what were the three plans generated in the demo?
retrieval_questions.a: The specs/ directory: replace-print-with-logging.md (chore), fix-sql-injection-vulnerabilities.md (bug), query-history-panel.md (feature, generated headlessly).

retrieval_questions.q: What sections does bug.md add beyond chore.md's plan format?
retrieval_questions.a: Bug Description (symptoms, expected vs actual), Problem Statement, Solution Statement, Steps to Reproduce, and Root Cause Analysis (plus surgical-fix/minimal-changes instructions).

retrieval_questions.q: What are Dan's three reasons for running fresh agent instances for every task?
retrieval_questions.a: (1) Free up context — focus every available token on one mission; (2) force prompts/plans/templates to be isolated, reusable, improvable assets with zero dependencies; (3) prepare for true off-device agentic coding.

retrieval_questions.q: Which KPIs does the fresh-agent pattern serve, and what's the context-window principle behind it?
retrieval_questions.a: Increase size of work handed off, decrease attempts, increase streak, decrease presence to zero — by decoupling performance from the conversational context window and aiming for one-shot successes.

retrieval_questions.q: How does a generated plan validate itself?
retrieval_questions.a: Every plan format ends with Validation Commands that must run with zero regressions (seeded with cd app/server && uv run pytest), the step-by-step tasks end by running them, and on camera the implement agent additionally reviewed its own git diff, found two issues, and fixed them unprompted.

retrieval_questions.q: Write the headless invocation Dan used for the feature template (flags matter).
retrieval_questions.a: claude -p "/feature \"<feature description>\"" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model opus --verbose > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl — a live-appending JSONL of system/assistant/tool events while the agent plans in the background.

retrieval_questions.q: What is 'think hard' in this lesson?
retrieval_questions.a: An information-dense keyword Anthropic encoded into Claude Code that activates the reasoning model — used in every template and in implement.md; one of the 12 leverage points (throw more compute at the problem).

retrieval_questions.q: What was the exact two-prompt structure that completed the logging chore?
retrieval_questions.a: /chore "Replace all server print statements with proper python logging..." (planning phase, fresh agent) then /implement specs/replace-print-with-logging.md (building phase, new fresh agent). 'This chore has been completed agentically with two prompts.'

retrieval_questions.q: Why does Dan say custom templates differentiate your engineering?
retrieval_questions.a: Off-the-shelf agents don't understand your codebase like you do and don't offer granular control across the SDLC; the more custom (specialized) your templates — per system, per class of bug, per page-set — the more unique your engineering and product become.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the lesson's call to action, and the named trap it warns against?
retrieval_questions.a: Don't wait — run one small /chore from the tac-3 codebase today to hit the aha moment. The trap: 'my codebase is too big / this won't work for my system' — a limiting belief; models will improve, tools will change.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Custom slash commands have grown frontmatter and dynamic context since recording
current_practice_gaps.why: The lesson's .claude/commands/*.md are plain markdown bodies with a single $ARGUMENTS slot. Current Claude Code commands support YAML frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools, model), positional $1/$2 arguments, inline !`bash` output injection, and @file references — so a 2026 chore.md could pin its own model and inject `git ls-files` output directly. The lesson's pattern still runs unchanged; the packaging got richer.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Templates were the proto-form of Agent Skills
current_practice_gaps.why: 'Template your engineering' — reusable, discoverable, improvable units of encoded process — is exactly what Claude Code later formalized as Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, auto-discovery, on-demand loading, bundled scripts). A modern reader should map template → skill for team-scale reuse, while noting slash-command templates remain the lighter-weight tool for repo-local plan generation.

current_practice_gaps.gap: 'think hard' magic keywords → first-class thinking controls
current_practice_gaps.why: Course-era Claude Code mapped the literal phrases think / think hard / ultrathink to escalating extended-thinking budgets. The words still work, but current practice exposes thinking as a first-class toggle/config and newer models manage reasoning budgets more autonomously. The transferable lever — deliberately buying more reasoning compute for planning-grade work — is unchanged.

current_practice_gaps.gap: --dangerously-skip-permissions is no longer the only headless posture
current_practice_gaps.why: The demo accepts full permission bypass for a low-risk planning run. Current Claude Code offers safer headless shapes: --allowedTools allowlists, permission modes, hooks as pre/post-tool gates, and sandboxed bash — plus the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) as the production embedding path with structured output and session control. stream-json remains real and is exactly how modern harnesses consume agents; Dan's 'low risk, for now' framing was honest and should be taught as scoping, not habit.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Model and UI drift: claude-opus-4-20250514 on screen
current_practice_gaps.why: The JSONL stream pins the era (Claude Opus 4, mid-2025); the TUI, todo rendering, and /install palette all look different today, and plan-mode now exists inside Claude Code as a native planning surface. Dan future-proofs in-lesson ('running on whatever the best model is... you're operating in the future, whatever your best model is, use that'); treat specifics as period detail. Notably, native plan mode complements rather than replaces this lesson: Dan's specs/-directory plans are durable, committable, team-shareable artifacts — a property ephemeral in-session plans still lack.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Fresh-agents doctrine predates today's context-engineering tooling
current_practice_gaps.why: Dan's manual new-terminal-per-task discipline anticipated what current tooling automates: /clear and /compact for context hygiene, subagents with isolated context windows, background tasks, and worktree-parallel agents. The lesson even name-drops 'isolated sub agent context windows' as a coming trick. The doctrine (one agent, one task, known context at boot, zero-dependency assets) transfers verbatim; only the mechanics got easier.

setup: Clone the course repo: git clone https://github.com/disler/tac-3.git && cd tac-3 (loot box link)

New terminal: sh ./scripts/start.sh — backend :8000, frontend :5173; upload users.json and run 'Show users with age between 20 and 40' to confirm the lesson-2 app works
reproduce_dan: Checkpoint 1 — meta prompt: in a FRESH Claude Code instance run /chore "Replace all server print statements with proper python logging. Use proper log levels. Preserve the exact same log output. Make sure all output is written to standard out". Pass when: a new plan exists in specs/ with all six Plan Format sections, and its Relevant Files inventory identifies the print statements in app/server/server.py and app/server/main.py (≈19 total; exact prose counts may vary run to run).

Checkpoint 2 — HOP execution: open a NEW instance and run /implement specs/<your-chore-plan>.md. Watch the todo list mirror the plan's Step by Step Tasks. Pass when: cd app/server && uv run pytest is green (37 pre-existing tests, zero regressions); grep -rn "print(" app/server --include="*.py" (excluding tests/) returns nothing in server.py; scripts/start.sh + a browser query shows the same [SUCCESS]/[ERROR] messages now emitted via logging.

Checkpoint 3 — bug template: commit your work, then in a fresh instance run /bug "Resolve major issue: our SQL statements are not being escaped — user input flows into SQL". Pass when the generated plan contains non-empty Steps to Reproduce and Root Cause Analysis sections that mention the keyword-blocklist weakness and f-string interpolation (server.py's DROP TABLE line and sql_processor's raw execute are on disk to find). Then /implement it in a NEW instance. Pass when: pytest is green with NEW injection-focused tests added (Dan's run: 18 new tests, 52 total — your counts will differ; require ≥1 new test file and zero regressions), and a malicious query attempt through the UI (e.g. asking for concatenated fields or a '); DROP TABLE users;-- style input) returns an error or safe result, never a schema change.

Checkpoint 4 — headless planning: write your own /feature one-liner (or reuse Dan's query-history-panel prompt), wrap it exactly as the video does — claude -p "/feature \"...\"" --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model <your-best-model> --verbose > feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl — and fire it from a plain terminal (not inside Claude Code). tail -f the JSONL while it runs. Pass when: the JSONL contains a system init event plus assistant/tool events, and a new feature plan appears in specs/ with User Story, phased Implementation Plan, Testing Strategy, and Acceptance Criteria — without you touching an interactive session. Do NOT implement it (matching Dan) unless you take the stretch.
stretch: S1 — Specialize a template: copy bug.md to a new command (e.g. bug-frontend.md) and dial its Instructions + Relevant Files to app/client/** only; run it against a UI-shaped bug description and diff the two generated plans to see encoding at work.

S2 — Write a HOP variant: create implement-and-review.md that implements the plan and then reviews the completed work against the plan, reporting any deviations before the final summary. Run it on your chore plan on a fresh branch and compare reports.

S3 — Port the pattern home: copy chore.md into a repo YOU own, rewrite ONLY the Relevant Files section and the pytest seed line in Validation Commands for that repo, then run one real small chore end-to-end (plan instance + implement instance). This is the lesson's explicit call to action.

S4 — Chain the phases: write a shell script that runs the claude -p planning command, waits, extracts the created spec path from the JSONL (or globs specs/), then launches a second claude -p run with /implement on it — a two-node ADW, hand-rolled, previewing lesson 4.

feature_plan_raw_agent_logs.jsonl exists, parses line-by-line as JSON, and corresponds to a spec file you did not interactively create
You can state, without notes: meta prompt vs HOP, the three fresh-agent reasons, and the five-part template anatomy
